# Handoff: the tools that take a project from a model file to G-code

**Status:** Working handoff, not committed. Written 2026-09-15 for the agent that implements the "journey" tools. The rules live in [the tool extension guide](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md); this document only sequences the work and records the decisions already made. When this document and the guide disagree, the guide wins and this document is wrong.

## Goal

Give the JusPrin agent, in-app and over MCP, every tool it needs to guide a user from opening a 3MF or importing an STL to a G-code file that prints well. That journey, from the guide's candidate catalog, is:

1. Get the model in and learn what it is.
2. Establish which printer, nozzle, plate, and filament will really do the job.
3. Capture intent, and end the back-and-forth by turning unknowns into visible assumptions.
4. Decide geometry: orientation, scale or units, split, repair, quantity, layout.
5. Mark local meaning: protect this hole, keep that face smooth, seam at the back.
6. Choose the technical method: process preset plus setting patches, including supports and adhesion.
7. Slice, read the report, look at the result, and iterate.
8. Export G-code and save the project with its intent, plan, and regions.

Out of scope: sending to a printer, preflight, live printing, camera, calibration, and everything under "Deliberately not tools" in the guide.

## Decisions already made; do not reopen them

- **Load every tool on every turn.** No enable-toolset tool, no tool search, no per-phase loading. The in-app adapter keeps the tools array byte-identical across a chat so OpenAI's prompt cache holds. Record the numbers (below) so the deferral decision can be made later on evidence. If you believe this is wrong for a concrete reason, stop and say so before building an alternative.
- **Tool shape follows the guide's "Tool budget and tool shape" section.** Domain operations, same-shape batches only, reads folded into sections. No tool that dispatches a list of unrelated commands.
- **Names and contracts come from the candidate catalog.** Do not invent new names. If a contract there proves impossible against the real Orca owner, change the guide in the same PR and say why.
- **Every tool follows the guide's implementation sequence and test matrix.** No registry entry backed only by the fake workspace.

## Scope: the 32 tools of the journey

| Toolset | Tools | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `core` | `workspace_inspect`, `object_analyze`, `settings_search`, `settings_get`, `settings_preview_patch`, `settings_apply_patch`, `intent_update`, `plan_set`, `slice_start`, `slice_report` | Five exist and are extended compatibly. |
| `project` | `project_open`, `project_save`, `project_attachment_read`, `history_restore` | `project_attachment_read` returns images; sequence it after the image projection exists. |
| `setup` | `presets_list`, `printer_setup_preview`, `printer_setup`, `printer_list` | |
| `geometry` | `object_place`, `plate_layout`, `object_import`, `object_import_file`, `project_delete_items` | Retires the three fixtures. |
| `reshape` | `object_divide_preview`, `object_divide`, `object_merge`, `object_repair` | |
| `regions` | `region_annotate` | Read back through `object_analyze` `regions`. |
| `check` | `view_render`, `slice_inspect`, `activity_cancel` | `view_render` prepare mode only. |
| `output` | `export_file` | G-code, sliced 3mf, project 3mf, STL, preset bundle. |

## Milestones

Each milestone ends with its eval passing against the real app, the guide's test matrix green for every tool it adds, and the catalog record in the guide updated. Do not start the next milestone's registry entries before the current milestone's real-adapter tests pass.

### M0: machinery every later milestone needs

- **Computation-only policy.** A registry declaration beside `ActionClass` that the coordinator honours; coordinator tests prove no card for `slice_start`, `activity_cancel`, `plan_set`, and a card for `slice_start` with `preempt: true`. Guide section "Computation-only mutations".
- **Output validator keywords.** Add `enum` and `maxLength` to `ToolRegistry::validate_output` with tests before any schema uses them. Guide section "Registry facts worth knowing".
- **JusPrin-owned stores.** Intent, plan, and region annotations in the 3mf auxiliary directory; confirmed printer facts in app data keyed by printer identity with expiry. Extend `ProjectStateDocument` ([ProjectStateDocument.hpp](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectStateDocument.hpp)) rather than adding a second persistence path; it already handles load, migration, and corruption. Add change reasons `Intent`, `Plan`, `Regions`, `PrinterFacts` to `ProjectStateChangeReason` in [ProjectState.hpp](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectState.hpp) and include them in `kInvalidatingReasons`. Provenance vocabulary per the guide section "JusPrin-owned project state".
- **Output schemas off the MCP wire.** `McpProtocol.cpp`

- The internal `record_*` tools are untouched.
- Remove any adapter-specific catalog or alias that appears during the work; the registry is the only definition source.
- Update the catalog record in the guide after every milestone so it stays the truth about what exists.

## MCP exposure requirements

- Every journey tool is `InApp | Mcp` except `object_import` (in-app) and `object_import_file` (MCP). Document the reason beside each definition.
- The stdio helper compiles the same registry; its offline `tools/list` must match the live list for the same build. The Python bridge tests in `tests/mcp` cover this.
- Legacy protocol projections in the bridge (`2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25`) must still produce a serialized text result for every new tool; add protocol fixtures per tool.
- MCP annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`) come from the action class; computation-only tools are still `readOnlyHint: false`.
- Path-taking tools (`project_open`, `project_save`, `object_import_file`, `export_file`) read or write the file only after approval, and the card shows the exact path. Test that the file is untouched on rejection.

## Testing requirements

Per tool, the guide's test matrix: registry, decoder, fake workspace ([FakeWorkspace.hpp](../../tests/jusprin_support/FakeWorkspace.hpp)), coordinator, real adapter ([OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp)), OpenAI projection, MCP projection, shell harness. Test files live in `tests/agent`, `tests/mcp`, and `tests/shell`. Build and run with the commands in the guide's "Verification commands" section.

Real OpenAI calls are required, not optional:

- Find the existing live multi-tool regression (start with `grep -rn -i live tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp`) and extend it with the final eval's transcript. It uses the key stored in AppConfig; do not paste a key into source or fixtures.
- For every live request, log the tools array byte size, `usage.input_tokens`, and the cached-token count OpenAI returns, and report them per milestone in the PR. This is the evidence the deferral decision depends on.
- Review each live transcript for wrong-tool selections and for questions the agent asked that the geometry did not justify. Both are eval failures.

Real MCP clients: one end-to-end Claude Code transcript per milestone through `jusprin-mcp`, with approvals taken in the rendered panel, not through a hidden decision hook. Use `--manual-mcp <temporary directory>`, never the user's data directory.


Baseline on 2026-09-15: five tools, 9,723 bytes, about 2,430 tokens, two thirds of it output schemas.

## Fork stewardship

Any line outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` follows [fork-stewardship.md](fork-stewardship.md). Expected seams in this handoff: the Measure feature-detection seam (M3), the load-path dialog choices (M2 and M3), and whatever `Plater` needs for slice completion and invalidation notifications (M1). Keep each additive, record the upstream lines touched, and include rebase evidence. The guide's "Upstream seams the tool system owns" section is updated in the same PR.

## Security gate

The guide's "Proportional security growth" section makes a review a gate before `export_file` (path write) and the computation-only exemption ship. Its minimum outcome is a written answer to each tripped trigger and the per-call approval evidence for every path tool. Do this in M6 before `export_file` merges; it is documentation and tests, not new infrastructure.

## What to report

In each milestone PR: the eval transcript, the test matrix evidence per tool with any "not applicable" layer explained, the measured catalog bytes and per-request token numbers, the upstream seams with rebase evidence, and anything left unverified stated plainly. Do not report a milestone done while any of these is missing.

## Open items that need Kenneth, not a guess

- Whether `project_attachment_read` and `view_render` ship in M6 or wait, since both depend on the image projection work in both adapters.
- Whether the settings allowlist in M4 should go further than the support, adhesion, seam, wall, infill, and shell keys, for example speed keys.
- The `gpt-5.4-mini` tool-search probe is deliberately not part of this handoff.

    The request, per the handoff: open a one-object STL (Orca's Cali Cat, 28.5 × 28.5 × 35 mm), say it is decorative, the front face will be visible, it must print in under five hours in PLA, and reach an exported G-code file with no manual setting edits and a slice without warnings.

    Over MCP pass

      Intent recorded, geometry analyzed, plan with decisions and assumptions recorded.

      One plan card held the face markings and the seam setting; both answered "queued", one click ran both.

      Slice: 1,824 s against the 18,000 s limit; 0 seams on the visible face, 274 of 296 on the hidden one; no warning that applies to a G-code print.

      Only the plan's own setting changed; the export was written after approval (950 KB). No dialog appeared.

    In the app, with OpenAI 1 of 7

      Runs 1–2The agent opened the STL by path, which ends the chat it came from, and the new project showed a card stuck on "running". A refusal also didn't say what was wrong. app bugs, fixed

      Run 3Tried to save the project over the .gcode path and skipped the plan step. app bug, fixed

      Runs 4, 5, 7Turned the cat onto its side (Orca's orientation score ranks that first), then exported a slice that warns of a floating cantilever. In run 7 the export card named the warning and the agent reported it. model choice

      Run 6Intent and plan recorded, import and slice approved on one card, cat left upright, 1,819 s, no warnings, no setting changes. pass

    Every run reached an exported file in two or three turns, with "Approved. Carry on." after each plan card. No run asked a question, which suits this model: nothing in its geometry makes a choice consequential.

      The slice report treats Bambu's print-dialog warnings the way Orca does: the bed-temperature one is dropped, the timelapse ones are marked as applying only to timelapse prints.

      An export card and its result list the slice's own warnings, so the person approving sees them.

      Saving the project to a non-.3mf path is refused before the card, pointing at the export tool.

      A plan's card stays disabled while the agent is still adding to it, and a decided or failed plan takes no new calls.

      plan_set no longer joins plans; a live run read "make these changes as one plan" as a call to it.

      Refused calls name the wrong values; the call that opened a project no longer shows in the project it opened.

      Both the in-app agent and MCP clients get one sentence on how a print request goes.

    Known limits

      In the app, the agent often trusts Orca's orientation score over the visible-face request and exports without reading the slice report. The tools report the problem truthfully; the model doesn't act on it.

```

  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
```

reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].

--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*

stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target

name: liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit
description: "RelWithDebInfo liblibslic3r_gui.a crossed Apple ar's 4 GiB archive limit on jusprin-newui (2026-09-13); CMAKE_AR override is ignored; manual llvm-ar relink recipe and its cd trap"
metadata:

On 2026-09-13, at jusprin-newui 770bd2b0a2 (after "Add the evidence-led Add a
printer flow"), a worktree RelWithDebInfo build failed archiving
`src/slic3r/RelWithDebInfo/liblibslic3r_gui.a`:
`Assertion failed: (memberOffset < 0xFFFFFFFF) ... ArchiveWriter.cpp` then
`fatal error in .../ranlib`. The archive llvm-ar produced was 4,309,350,176
bytes; the main checkout's copy built minutes earlier was 4,143,827,796 and
still fit. Objects are big because the root CMakeLists.txt (lines ~544-548)
rewrites RelWithDebInfo -O2 to -O0 on purpose. Disk space was not the cause.

**Why:** the failed build left the OLD harness binary in place, and the harness
runs afterwards "passed" against stale code (a new `--printer-setup` flag
silently ran the default mode: same 285 check count). Gate runs on build
success and compare binary mtime.

**How to apply:**
- `-DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar` on an existing build dir does
  nothing: `CMakeFiles/<ver>/CMakeCXXCompiler.cmake` sets CMAKE_AR as a normal
  variable that shadows the cache.
- Working relink: `ninja -f build-RelWithDebInfo.ninja -t commands <target>`,
  drop compile lines, swap ar/ranlib for llvm-ar/llvm-ranlib on the gui archive
  line only, then run EACH line in its own `(cd build/arm64 && eval "$line")`.
  One `sh` script fails with bogus "no such file" errors because the
  encoding-check line does `cd src/slic3r` and it leaks; `sh -e` also does not
  stop inside `&&` chains. Apple's linker accepted the >4 GiB llvm-ar archive.

  checkout's build/arm64 cache has llvm-ar (commit 449b676145 documents it in
  agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md); any newly configured build dir
  gets Apple ar and fails again. Configure new dirs with the flags in
  [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

  4,308,513,464 bytes). Shortcut that worked: after the failed build, from
  `-t commands shell_integration_harness` drop lines containing ` -c `; only
  the last two remain relevant (gui archive, then harness link). Run just
  those two, swapping ar/ranlib on the archive line. Harness then passed.

name: background-bash-timeout-kills-builds
description: "A run_in_background Bash build dies at the tool timeout (ninja prints \"interrupted by user\", exit 130); launch long builds with nohup and watch the log instead"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8c1e8dd3-1475-48e9-9398-2d5eaa424bab
  modified: 2026-09-14T19:01:34.576Z
---

A `cmake --build` started with the Bash tool's `run_in_background` is still
bound by that call's `timeout` (default 120 s, max 600 s). When it fires the
build log ends with `ninja: build stopped: interrupted by user.` and `exit=130`,
which looks like a human Ctrl-C but is the harness. Seen 2026-09-14 on a
725-step JusPrin rebuild.

**Why:** the notification says "completed" and the log shows no compiler
error, so it is easy to misread as a finished build; the changed files had not
compiled at all.

**How to apply:** for anything longer than a few minutes, start it detached
(`nohup sh -c "cmake --build … > log 2>&1; echo exit=\$? >> log" & disown`),
then arm a Monitor on the log that reports progress and the `exit=` line. Check
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' log` before trusting the result. Related:
[[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

name: live-test-built-app-on-mac
description: "How to launch, see, and drive the locally built JusPrin app on the Mac: the shared bundle id binds tools to the wrong instance, and \"on another Space\" usually means the window is on the second monitor, not that the user is in full screen."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: fa2d66ed-e217-440b-aae0-da4164953edc
  modified: 2026-09-09T16:51:11.156Z
---

Every build of the fork (and /Applications/OrcaSlicer.app) shares bundle id `com.softfever3d.orca-slicer`. The desktop-control tools resolve an app by bundle id and bind to whichever instance comes first, so `app_list_windows` returns `[]` and filtered screenshots hide the window you actually launched.

**Working recipe (2026-09-05):** `ditto` the built .app into the scratchpad, `plutil -replace CFBundleIdentifier -string com.jusprin.worktree-test`, `codesign --force --deep -s -`, then `open -n <copy>.app --args <model>` and `request_access` for the new id. `app_screenshot`/`app_click` then work and include popup menus. A display-scope `left_click` on the header did NOT open the fork's PopupWindow menus, but a background `app_click` did; take the pixel-level `zoom` with the display tools afterwards (call `app_release` first). Display-scope `Escape` does not close those popups; a click elsewhere does.

The MCP discovery file `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/jusprin/mcp.json` points at the newest instance's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`; `tests/mcp/probe.py`'s `call()` can drive real tools (e.g. `workspace_inspect`, then `report_slice_review` with sessionId/plateId/sliceResultId) to put the header into the Check-print state without lldb. lldb `expr` cannot call inline accessors like `status_row()`.

**Why:** On 2026-09-01 a verification pass screenshotted the stock app instead of the build; on 2026-09-05 the tools bound to another session's main-repo build.

**How to apply:** Confirm the pid with `pgrep -fl OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS`; never kill an instance you did not launch. `osascript` System Events by unix id still works to set `frontmost`. See [[jusprin-shell-phase-1-design]] and [[orca-inherited-teardown-crash]].

**"On another Space" usually means "on the other monitor."** Cost about ten turns on
2026-09-09 and produced a wrong report to Kenneth. `app_list_windows` returns
`is_off_space: true` and clicks are refused with "this window is on another Space";
`app_bring_to_current_space` then fails with "the user's current Space is a full-screen
app." Both messages are about Spaces, so the natural read is that the user is sitting in
a full-screen app — but with *Displays have separate Spaces* on, a window merely sitting
on the second monitor produces exactly the same symptoms. Kenneth was not in full screen;
the harness had opened on the Acer.

Tell them apart before saying anything to the user: take a **display-scope** screenshot
(`app_release`, then `computer_batch` screenshot). Its header names the monitor it
captured and lists the others — if the window shows up there, it is a monitor problem,
not a Space problem, and the display-scope tools can drive it immediately. Never conclude
"the user is in a full-screen app" from the background tools' error text alone.

The same flag also flaps: a window can read `is_off_space: false` and click fine, then
read `true` a minute later. Clicks delivered while it is true report `ok ... unverified`
and silently do nothing. **A click that reports "unverified" and changes nothing is not
evidence of an application bug** — on 2026-09-09 that nearly became a filed defect about
being unable to retry after a failed MCP connect. Re-verify on a reachable window before
concluding anything about the app.

**Prefer the shell harness over a re-signed app copy for Agent-panel work.**
`tests/shell/.../JusPrinShellHarness.app` already carries its own bundle id
(`io.jusprin.shell-harness`), so none of the bundle-id collision above applies, and
`--manual-unconfigured` lands directly on the dock's not-set-up state — one click from
the Agent setup chooser. Build target is `shell_integration_harness`, not `shell_harness`.

**Isolate `$HOME` when testing MCP client setup.** `Mcp::default_catalog_paths()` reads
`$HOME`, so the flow will happily rewrite the real `~/.cursor/mcp.json`. Launch with
`HOME=<scratch>` holding a `.cursor/mcp.json` fixture; detection, the diff, and the write
all follow it. Force a write failure with `chmod 444` on the file **and** `555` on its
directory — the directory alone is not enough.

**Re-signed copies trigger system prompts.** Each rebuild + ad-hoc re-sign changes the cdhash, so macOS re-asks for Downloads access (recent-project thumbnail load blocks in `fopen`) and Keychain access (agent runtime reads the API key). Both are prompts only the user can answer. Avoid them by running the binary directly (`nohup <copy>.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer --datadir <scratch copy of JusPrin2 with recent_projects cleared> <model>`) with `OPENAI_API_KEY=<placeholder>` in the environment, which short-circuits the Keychain lookup in `AgentConfiguration.cpp`. Use `sample <pid>` on the main thread to see which prompt is blocking.

**Give each automated harness run a fresh scratch `$HOME`.** On 2026-09-09 a second run
against a reused scratch `$HOME` (and with a `jusprin-mcp` helper left over from the
first) never got past the Agent page handshake: it printed `HARNESS WAIT
agent_bridge_handshake preview=0 plate=0 slice_valid=1` about twice a second forever and
had to be killed at ten minutes. Runs before and after it, each with a freshly created
`$HOME` and a `pkill -f jusprin-mcp` first, finished with zero `HARNESS WAIT` lines at
all. **The cause was not isolated** — reuse and the stale helper were not separated, so
treat this as a recipe, not an explanation. `rm -rf` and recreate the scratch `$HOME`,
`pkill -f jusprin-mcp`, then run; if the handshake wait appears anyway, kill it early
rather than assuming the change under test broke the bridge.

description: "A background subagent that \"waits for the build notification\" ends its turn and is gone; tell agents to block on long builds in the foreground and never end a turn with work pending."
metadata:

On 2026-09-10 a measurement subagent kicked off a 700-step JusPrin rebuild in
the background, then ended its turn with "I'll wait for the completion
notification." Subagents get no notifications after they stop, and SendMessage
was unavailable, so the parent had to babysit the ninja PID and run the
harness itself.

**Why:** a subagent's turn is its whole life. Anything it defers to "later"
never happens. The parent cannot resume it without SendMessage.

**How to apply:** in every Agent prompt for work that includes a build or any
long step, say explicitly: run long commands in the foreground with a long
timeout (up to 600000 ms per call, loop `until` the PID exits if longer), and
never end the turn while a step is still running or a result is still
pending. If the agent stops early anyway, check `ps` for its build process,
wait on the PID, and finish its plan from its scratch files. See
[[subagent-worktrees-create-manually]] and [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]].

        "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {},

        "MCP-Protocol-Version": PROTOCOL_VERSION,
        "Mcp-Method": method,

    if "name" in params:

    with closing(http.client.HTTPConnection(endpoint.hostname, endpoint.port, timeout=310)) as connection:

Yes, the review is done. The branch builds and most automated tests pass, but I found three test failures the dev's report doesn't mention, plus several code defects. I wouldn't merge it as is.

## Test results (macOS, branch tip `ae5f2d7c4c`)

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Full build (970 steps) | Pass |
| Agent unit tests | Pass (213 cases) |
| Other JusPrin unit tests (4 suites) | Pass |
| Agent page tests | Pass (133) |
| App harness: default, stock, MCP, MCP-helper modes | All pass |
| Python MCP helper tests | **1 failure** |
| Workspace adapter harness | **Crashes on exit** |
| Live OpenAI regression | **Failed in 3 of 3 full runs, plus a 4th debug run cut short at the same stall** (base branch: passed 1 of 1) |

- **Python test:** the helper returns tools 25 at a time, and the branch now has 31. The Linux packaging test (`tests/mcp/test_linux_package.py:70`) still expects all 31 on the first page. It's a test bug, but the report calls these tests green.
- **Harness crash:** every check passes, then the process segfaults on exit (exit 139), every time. A Windows fix merged into this branch now closes the main window to quit, and on macOS a web view's delayed setup callback then runs after the view is destroyed. The base branch exits cleanly.
- **Live regression:** in 3 of 4 runs, the harness got stuck waiting after the agent proposed an ordinary settings change. Temporary logging (since removed) showed why:
  - The model added a plan ID to that single change on its own, so the app answered "queued in plan" and showed a plan card instead of a normal card.
  - The harness clicks Reject on the normal card, finds nothing, and waits until its deadline.
  - This is also a behaviour change users will see: the model now sometimes wraps single changes in plans.
  - The one run that got past this step failed later: both plan changes were reported as succeeded, but the two settings didn't hold the planned values. Settings changes that change nothing are also reported as success, which may be related. I didn't find the cause.

## Code defects found in review
From reading the code; the time-regex bug I also confirmed myself.
1. **A slice finishing fails other approval cards that are still waiting.** This includes the agent's own no-card slice. It also breaks a plan that slices and then continues.
2. **Plan IDs aren't scoped per chat or client.** If an MCP client and the in-app agent both use a plan ID like `plan-1`, "Approve all" on the MCP card also runs the in-app changes, which that card never showed.
3. **A plan member that fails or is cancelled before approval leaves the rest approvable**, so the user can run a partial plan.
4. **The agent can't open or import any STEP file.** The tool auto-cancels Orca's STEP mesh dialog, which aborts the load; opening a project first clears the current one, leaving it empty.
5. **`discard_unsaved` doesn't discard** when the user once chose "remember: save". The project is silently saved, or an unanswered file dialog blocks the call.
6. **The preset export overwrites existing files** after the first clash, even with overwrite off.
7. **The print-time parser reads ordinary words as time.** "gram", "team" and "seam" each count as one minute.
8. **Smaller ones:**
   - A repair that fails halfway leaves the model changed without a refresh.
   - Splitting an object can open Orca's "Disable Auto-Drop?" dialog.
   - Mirrored parts come out inside-out in exported STLs and region markers.
   - Card titles are cut mid-character (can throw on non-English names) and can hide the file path the spec requires on the card.

## Spec conformance
All 32 tools exist with the right names. The three old placeholder tools are gone, and the changes to Orca-owned files are small and recorded in the guide. The gaps:
- **MCP evals:** the spec requires a Claude Code transcript with approvals clicked in the panel. The dev used a scripted client, citing "the owner's instruction to use OpenAI only", which appears nowhere in the spec or guide. The M3 and M5 evals approved through the hidden decision hook the spec forbids.
- **Decisions reserved for you:** the dev added speed settings to the allowlist and shipped `view_render` and `project_attachment_read` without a recorded decision from you.
- **M0 change reasons:** the four new reasons were never added. The dev argued the rule can't work as written and left it "open" in the guide.
- **Missing evidence:** no per-tool legacy-protocol fixtures, no M6 token numbers, and no M1, M2 or M4 MCP evals as specified.
- **Branch hygiene:** it carries unrelated commits (chat titles, Windows harness and Mesa fixes) plus a merge commit. It's 6 commits behind `jusprin-newui` (the report says 4), but merges without conflicts.

I didn't reproduce defect 1 in the running app: you declined screen access, and approving plans needs panel clicks. The review worktree is `.claude/worktrees/journey-tools-review` with a full build. I haven't used the app by hand. Every test I ran launched the real built app, but through its automated test harness, which clicks the Agent panel with scripts. The live OpenAI runs were among those. You declined screen access, so I couldn't click through it myself, and I haven't done the dev's journey eval myself (open an STL, ask for a print, export G-code).

Everything below uses the build in my review worktree, which is on the dev's branch. I just rebuilt the test harness, so it no longer has my temporary logging. Each option keeps its settings in a scratch folder, not in your real JusPrin data.

## Option 1: the full app with a scratch settings folder
```bash
mkdir -p ~/jusprin-review-data && cp -R ~/Library/Application\ Support/JusPrin2/. ~/jusprin-review-data/
```
```bash

```
- The copy brings your printers and your saved OpenAI key, so the Agent panel works straight away.
- Running the binary directly avoids the Keychain and Downloads permission prompts that a copied `.app` triggers.
- To try the journey, attach an STL in the Agent panel and ask something like: "this is decorative, the front face will be visible, under five hours in PLA, give me G-code".

## Option 2: the agent over MCP, driven from Claude Code
Start the app in the harness's "leave it open for MCP clients" mode:
```bash
/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/journey-tools-review/build/arm64/tests/shell/RelWithDebInfo/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --manual-mcp ~/jusprin-review-mcp
```

Then register this build's MCP helper with Claude Code, pointed at that folder's connection file:

- This is the eval the spec asked for: Claude Code makes the requests, and you click Approve or Reject in the app's panel.
- It opens a two-plate test project.
- Use a new name like `jusprin-review` so your existing `jusprin` server stays pointed at your normal build.

## Option 3: repeat my automated runs
```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=<your key> /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/journey-tools-review/build/arm64/tests/shell/RelWithDebInfo/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --live-agent
```

Two cautions:
- **Opening a project from chat ends that chat,** a limit the dev's report notes; attaching the file avoids it.
- **The agent can't open STEP files** (defect 4 in my review), so use STL or 3MF.

## Fix before merge
1. **The live OpenAI test fails in 3 of 4 runs** (reproduced). The model sometimes wraps a single settings change in a plan, so the user sees "queued" and a plan card instead of a normal approval card. The fix is to accept a plan ID only when a plan has more than one change, or to stop offering it on single changes. The test should then pass reliably.
2. **The workspace harness crashes on exit on macOS** (reproduced every run). The Windows fix merged into this branch now closes the window to quit, and a web view's delayed callback then runs after the view is gone. It's test-only, but it makes that suite fail by exit code.
3. **The Python packaging test fails** (reproduced). It expects all 31 tools on the first page, but the helper returns 25 per page. The fix is to follow the page cursor in the test.
4. **A slice finishing fails other approval cards that are still waiting** (from reading). The agent's own slice can cancel the user's pending cards, and a plan that slices and then continues breaks.
5. **"Approve all" on one plan card can run changes it never showed** (from reading). Plan IDs aren't scoped per chat or client, so an MCP plan and an in-app plan with the same ID merge. This is an approval bypass, so it's the most important one to fix.
6. **The agent can't open STEP files** (from reading). The tool auto-cancels Orca's STEP mesh dialog, which aborts the load. Opening a project first clears the current one, so the user is left with an empty project.

# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

**Grouped approvals (M7).** The registry adds an optional `planId` (1 to 64 characters) to every mutation's schema except `plan_set` (`joins_plans`), so those tools use non-strict function calling; `validate_call` checks it, refuses it on a read, keeps it away from the tool's own decoder and puts it back for the coordinator, which records it on the activity (saved in `state.json`, sent to the page as `planId`). A member always waits for approval, including a computation-only call that would otherwise run without a card. `plan_set` is left out because a live run read "make these changes as one plan" as a call to it with a `planId`, and grouping the agent's own words adds nothing to the card. Both adapters answer a member at once instead of waiting for the card, because the person can decide only after the agent has proposed the rest: the in-app agent gets `{"state":"queued", "planId", "actionId", "message"}` as its function output, and an MCP client gets the same text with no `structuredContent` (it is not the tool's result; `_meta["io.jusprin/activity"].state` is `queued`). The server advertises no `outputSchema`, so no client expects structured content from it. The outcome is read later from the new `activities` section of `workspace_inspect` (the latest 20 calls with state, plan and error). `approve` or `reject` on any member decides every waiting member; `pump` runs a plan's members in proposal order, one at a time, and holds a later member while an earlier one is still running (a slice that waits). Staleness for a member counts only changes from outside the plan: a change that arrives while another member of the same plan executes does not count, and any other content or settings change after approval fails the next member as `stale_revision`. Settings patches in a plan skip the revision half of their own guard for the same reason; the confirmed before-values still guard every key. A member that fails fails the plan's remaining approved members as `plan_step_failed`; members already done stay done. The page draws one card per plan beneath the message that proposed its first member (and in the external-tools area for MCP plans), titled with the latest `plan_set` headline, listing each member with its state, naming the member that makes the plan destructive, with one Approve all / Reject all that sends the decision for the first waiting member. While the in-app agent's turn is still streaming, those buttons are disabled ("The Agent is still adding to this plan"), so a person cannot approve half a plan. An MCP plan has no such signal; its card is live as soon as its first member arrives.

A plan takes members only while its card is undecided and none of its calls has failed; a later call with that `planId` is refused as `plan_closed` (a live run proposed a member after the plan's first call had already failed stale). The coordinator's own error codes for plans are `plan_closed` and `plan_step_failed`.

An agent that records its plan between previewing and applying would break its own call. The edit feed (`WorkspaceEditHub`) is the precedent for a feed that reports a change without advancing the revision. Decide per kind: a region annotation generates Orca artifacts and is a real project change; an intent answer or a plan statement is not.
